tagline: The southern Caribbean's cruise capital — a Platinum Coast within electric range, and the Windwards one hybrid hop away.
summary: Barbados is the eastern anchor of the southern Caribbean: Bridgetown's port welcomed roughly 818,000 cruise arrivals in 2025 on top of a record 727,000 long-stay visitors, and the island's celebrated west ('Platinum') coast — Carlisle Bay, Holetown, Sandy Lane, Port St Charles — runs in a sheltered 12 nm ribbon north of the harbour. Today that coast is served by diesel catamaran day-cruises and taxi transfers on a congested coastal highway; there is no scheduled sea link at all to St Vincent, the Grenadines or St Lucia, each about 95 nm away. A foiling fleet turns the harbour, the west coast and ultimately the Windward chain into one smooth, quiet network.

use_cases.title: Cruise-pier to Platinum Coast in one hop
use_cases.body: Meet ships at Port Barbados and fly guests up the sheltered west coast to Holetown, Mullins and Port St Charles — replacing the taxi crawl up Highway 1 with a 20-minute foiling arrival at a marina berth.

use_cases.title: Sandy Lane / Port Ferdinand private shuttle
use_cases.body: A quiet, zero-emission tender service for the island's villa and marina-residence clientele — Carlisle Bay sunset runs, restaurant hops to The Cliff and Lone Star, and airport-to-marina arrivals without the road.

use_cases.title: Bridgetown harbour & south-coast link
use_cases.body: A scheduled Careenage ↔ Carlisle Bay ↔ Oistins service puts the island's restaurant and fish-fry corridor on the water, relieving the south-coast road at peak hours.

use_cases.title: The Windwards corridor
use_cases.body: Barbados ↔ St Vincent / Bequia (~95 nm) and Barbados ↔ St Lucia (~97 nm): the first scheduled sea links from Barbados into the Grenadines island-hopping spine, no charging infrastructure required on the far shore.

journeys.today: A taxi or tour bus up the busy west-coast highway — 40–60 minutes in traffic for a 10 nm straight shot along one of the Caribbean's most beautiful coasts.
journeys.with_navier: A ~10 nm foiling run up the Platinum Coast — flat, silent, spray-free — arriving directly at the marina pontoon in about 25 minutes.

journeys.today: The south-coast road crawls on Friday evenings; visitors queue for taxis both ways.
journeys.with_navier: A ~6 nm hop around Needham's Point to Oistins Bay — an evening water-shuttle that turns the island's signature night out into part of the experience.

journeys.today: No ferry exists — the only option is a regional flight via Argyle or multiple hops, then a boat transfer.
journeys.with_navier: A direct ~95 nm hybrid foiling crossing from Bridgetown into the Grenadines sailing grounds — smooth through the Atlantic channel swell that makes conventional small craft impractical here.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The whole island is a Pioneer II market: Bridgetown ↔ Port St Charles is ~10 nm, Carlisle Bay ↔ Oistins ~6 nm, and the full west-coast mesh of beach stops (Brandons, Brighton, Mullins, Little Good Harbour) sits in a 1–12 nm band — multiple rotations per charge on the sheltered Caribbean side of the island.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR (700 nm hybrid, no shore-charging dependency) opens the inter-island layer no operator serves today: Barbados ↔ St Vincent (~94 nm), Barbados ↔ St Lucia (~97 nm), and onward reach down the Grenadines to Grenada — connecting this brief to the st-lucia-grenadines network.

competitive_landscape: The water is already a product here — just not a transport network. Diesel sail-and-power catamarans (Tiami, Cool Runnings, Jolly Roger, Good Times) run daily lunch, snorkel and sunset cruises along the west coast, and glass-bottom and dive boats work Carlisle Bay's wrecks; that is strong evidence visitors pay to be on this water every day. But point-to-point movement — cruise pier to resort, hotel to restaurant, island to island — remains entirely road and air. No scheduled passenger sea service connects Barbados to its neighbours.

precedents.what: ~$100M, ~100-vessel electric foiling network with JIH Global, 3-year phased rollout, first 5 vessels in 2026
precedents.why_it_matters: The playbook for a resort-island nation: the same fleet model maps onto Barbados' cruise-plus-resort coast and the Windwards corridor.

seasonality: Year-round operating season. The west and south coasts are in the lee of the island — sheltered Caribbean water — while the brisk easterly trades (strongest Dec–Jun) build chop offshore and on the Atlantic side; foiling flies above the trade-wind chop that conventional catamarans plough through. Hurricane season (Jun–Nov) historically touches Barbados less than islands further north, but scheduling flexibility matters Aug–Oct.
regulatory_note: Port and harbour operations run through Barbados Port Inc. (Port Barbados, the Shallow Draught and the Careenage) with maritime oversight from the Barbados Maritime Transport Administration. Barbados is a vocal small-island climate leader — the Bridgetown Initiative and a national 2030 renewable-energy goal give a clean-fleet marine service direct policy resonance — and the government is actively courting marine-tourism investment.
